Cypress
sī´prĕs
n. (a hard evergreen timber tree)
From the Greek kuparissos, through the Latin cupressus. The Hebrew tirzah occurs once. It is named in Isaiah's account of how an idol is manufactured, standing between the cedar and the oak in the carpenter's choice of stock.

Biblical Definition

The word stands once, and it stands in the middle of the most devastating description of idol-making in Scripture: “He heweth him down cedars, and taketh the cypress and the oak, which he strengtheneth for himself among the trees of the forest: he planteth an ash, and the rain doth nourish it” (Isaiah 44:14). Isaiah is deliberately slow here. He follows the timber from the seedling that God's own rain waters, through the felling, to the workshop, and he will not let the reader skip a step, because every step indicts the workman. The same log serves two purposes: “Then shall it be for a man to burn: for he will take thereof, and warm himself; yea, he kindleth it, and baketh bread; yea, he maketh a god, and worshippeth it; he maketh it a graven image, and falleth down thereto” (Isaiah 44:15). Half the tree cooks his dinner; the other half receives his prayers. The prophet then records the prayer itself: “And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god” (Isaiah 44:17). The poor man's version is described with the same irony: “He that is so impoverished that he hath no oblation chooseth a tree that will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman to prepare a graven image, that shall not be moved” (Isaiah 40:20). Cypress was chosen because it lasts. That is the whole argument the idolater has.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines cypress as a genus of trees, the wood of which is remarkably durable, and the tree an emblem of mourning.

expand to see more

CYPRESS, n. A genus of trees, the wood of which is very durable; the branches were formerly used at funerals, hence it is an emblem of mourning.

CEDAR, n. A large evergreen tree of the genus Juniperus or Pinus, valuable for its durable timber.

OAK, n. A tree of the genus Quercus, of great strength and durability.

IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.

GRAVEN, pp. Carved; engraved; cut, as an image, in wood, stone or metal.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 44:14 — "He heweth him down cedars, and taketh the cypress and the oak, which he strengtheneth for himself among the trees of the forest: he planteth an ash, and the rain doth nourish it."

Isaiah 44:15 — "Then shall it be for a man to burn: for he will take thereof, and warm himself; yea, he kindleth it, and baketh bread; yea, he maketh a god, and worshippeth it; he maketh it a graven image, and falleth down thereto."

Isaiah 44:17 — "And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god."

Isaiah 40:20 — "He that is so impoverished that he hath no oblation chooseth a tree that will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman to prepare a graven image, that shall not be moved."

Modern Corruption

Idolatry is redefined as a primitive stage of religion outgrown by modern man, which conceals the fact that Isaiah's workman is a sophisticate reasoning about durable materials.

expand to see more

The standard modern treatment of Isaiah 44 files it under the religion of the ancient Near East and leaves it there: people once believed statues were alive, and we no longer do, so the chapter has antiquarian interest only. This misses Isaiah's actual charge. His idolater is not a credulous primitive; he is a man making reasonable decisions about timber. He selects cypress because cypress resists rot. He hires a cunning workman. He is attentive, practical, and economical — and at the end of an entirely rational process he addresses a piece of wood as my god. The prophet's point is that idolatry is not a failure of intelligence but a corruption of the heart, which is why intelligence never cures it.

The second corruption is a churchly one. Because the passage mocks carved images, Protestants have often read it as a text about other people, finished business, a sin the Reformation settled. Calvin's judgment is the sounder one: the human heart is a perpetual factory of idols, and it does not require a workshop. What Isaiah exposes is the mechanism — taking something God made and given, dividing it, and assigning to one part of it the trust that belongs to God alone. A career, a family, a reputation, a doctrine of one's own devising, each can be the residue of the log. The material has changed; the transaction is identical.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tirzah (H8645), a species of hard tree; erez (H730), cedar; allon (H437), oak; pesel (H6459), a graven image.

expand to see more

Hebrew tirzah (H8645) — a durable tree, rendered cypress; only Isaiah 44:14.

Hebrew erez (H730) — cedar, the great timber of Lebanon.

Hebrew allon (H437) — oak, the third tree in the workman's selection.

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image, an idol carved from wood or stone.

Hebrew charash (H2796) — a craftsman, the cunning workman hired in Isaiah 40:20.

Usage

"“Taketh the cypress and the oak” — the idolater selecting his stock."

"“He maketh a god, and worshippeth it” — the second half of the same log."

"“Chooseth a tree that will not rot” — durability as the idol's only credential."
